User: I'm going through a legal process and need to organize my thoughts. The case involves nondisclosure agreement dispute. My lawyer is Lisa Park with Park Legal Group; we have proceedings at the federal district court. We're past the filing stage and waiting for the court calendar.. Opposing party: my former landlord. This is in King County, Washington. The contract was signed last year and they've since stopped performing. Can you help me figure out what to ask my attorney about what documents I should bring and what to say in the hearing? I want to be ready for the legal next steps.
Assistant: Good — I can help you get organized. I’m not a lawyer, so treat these as practical preparation and questions to run by Lisa Park. If you’d like, I can also draft a one‑page checklist, an email to Lisa, or a short script for what you might say in court — tell me which.

Suggested documents to bring (organized, tabbed, and in both paper and a USB/pdf):
- Core contract and proof of execution
  - Signed nondisclosure agreement (original or a clear copy) and any amendments.
  - Any cover letters or signing confirmations.
- Communications showing the breach/nonperformance
  - Emails, text messages, letters, portal messages between you and the landlord referring to the NDA or the confidential material.
  - Any notices, demands, or requests you sent about performance.
- Timeline and summary
  - One‑page, chronological timeline of events with dates and one‑line description of each event.
- Evidence of harm/damages
  - Financial records (bank statements, invoices, receipts) showing losses or costs resulting from the landlord’s conduct.
  - Any valuations, lost‑opportunity documents, or estimates of remediation costs.
- Corroborating documents
  - Leases, rent payment records, repair requests, inspection reports, photos/videos, security camera stills (if relevant).
  - Witness contact details and short statements (name, relationship, what they can attest to).
- Discovery and court filings
  - Copies of every court filing to date (complaint, exhibits, motions, responses), plus the docket number and any orders.
  - Discovery responses, interrogatories, production logs, deposition transcripts (if any).
- Settlement/negotiation records
  - Any settlement offers, mediation docs, or correspondence discussing resolution.
- Confidentiality/protective materials
  - Anything you consider confidential that may need sealing or a protective order.
- Evidence authenticity support
  - Metadata or screenshots showing timestamps, chain of custody notes, and any witness who can authenticate electronic messages.
- Practical items
  - Government ID, business card, notebook, pen, and extra copies of key exhibits for the court and opposing counsel.
  - USB drive with organized PDFs (same tab order as paper binders).

How to organize exhibits:
- Number or letter exhibits (Exhibit 1 — NDA; Ex. 2 — timeline; Ex. 3 — email chain).
- Include a one‑sentence exhibit description on a cover page.
- Prepare an index/table of contents and bring at least three sets of copies (court, opposing counsel, your attorney).

Questions to ask Lisa Park (prioritize what you want answered at your next meeting):
Case status & schedule
- What’s the next court date and what will occur then (status conference, pretrial, motion hearing)?
- Expected timeline for the court calendar and likely next procedural steps?
Hearing logistics & format
- Will this be a live hearing, telephone/Zoom, or a status conference? Will the judge take evidence that day or only set dates?
- Will I need to testify at this hearing or only appear for scheduling/argument?
Evidence & exhibits
- Which documents does the court expect to see at this stage? Which documents should I bring personally?
- Do we need to pre‑mark exhibits or file an exhibit list before the hearing?
- Any documents that should be submitted under seal or require a protective order?
Witnesses & testimony
- Should I bring any witnesses to the hearing? If so, who and what should they be prepared to say?
- Do you want me to prepare an affidavit, witness statement, or summary for the file?
Legal strategy & motions
- Are there pending motions (motions in limine, summary judgment, discovery motions) we should expect?
- Are there immediate tasks we should complete (e.g., additional discovery, subpoenas, expert reports)?
Settlement & alternatives
- Is settlement/motion to mediate advisable before the next stage? What’s our negotiation posture?
Practicalities & preparation
- How should I testify if called? Any talking points or things I must avoid saying?
- How should I organize the documents and notes you want me to bring to a prep session?
Fees & costs
- Estimated costs to prepare for the next phase (depositions, experts, filing fees).
- Any billing considerations for additional prep or court appearances.
Privilege & confidentiality concerns
- What communications should I avoid sharing publicly or on social media?
- How do we protect confidential information in filings and at the hearing?
Other specifics
- Are there local rules for the Western District of Washington (formatting, exhibit rules, chambers procedures) we must follow?
- Anything specific to King County circumstances we should consider?

What to say in the hearing (if you must speak or testify) — short practice tips and a sample brief statement:
General tips for testimony or addressing the court:
- Address the judge as “Your Honor.”
- Speak slowly and audibly; keep answers short and factual.
- Do not volunteer extra information — answer the question asked.
- If you don’t understand a question, say so and ask for clarification.
- Stick to first‑hand facts; avoid speculation or arguing your interpretation of law.
- Review and rehearse your timeline and the specific dates/communications.
Sample brief statement (if asked to summarize or give a short factual statement):
- “Good morning, Your Honor. My name is [Your Name]. I’m here regarding Case No. [XXXX]. I signed a nondisclosure agreement with [landlord name] on [date]. Since [approx date], they disclosed/failed to protect/confidentially [describe the act briefly], and they have stopped performing obligations under the agreement. I’ve brought the contract, the relevant communications, and documentation of my damages for the court and opposing counsel. I’m prepared to answer questions or provide any specific documents the court requests.”
(Use only as a concise factual intro; Lisa should review and tailor this.)

Preparation steps to do now:
- Create the one‑page timeline and an exhibit index.
- Compile, scan, and label all documents into a single PDF and folder structure.
- Highlight or annotate the most important passages of the NDA and key emails.
- Meet with Lisa for a focused witness prep session and at least one mock direct/cross exam if you’ll testify.
- Confirm with Lisa which documents to file and whether anything needs sealing.
- Check travel, courthouse procedures, and arrive early on the hearing day.

What I can do next for you
- Draft a one‑page exhibit checklist and hearing script for you to print.
- Draft an email or list of the above questions to send to Lisa Park.
- Create a printable timeline template for you to fill in.

Would you like me to draft a short email to Lisa Park with these questions and attach your checklist and timeline template? If yes, tell me whether to keep it formal and whether to include any specific case number or attachments.
